title: Etta the Judge's Heart
markdown:
The sun peeked over the green hills and dappled the meadow with gold. Etta the fox, fur like warm toast, smoothed her apron. It was the Great Meadow Bake-Off. She loved baking; judging felt trickier. How did you measure a baker’s heart? The theme was being fair to every crumb.

Noor the rabbit hopped over. “Ready?” Beside her waddled Miss Penny the hedgehog. “My blueberry buns have ten blueberries each.” Etta smiled. Her paws felt shaky anyway. Choosing between stars and a rainbow would have been easier than a scorecard.

A squirrel blew a whistle: pip-pip-peep. Bakers lined up. Etta’s apron showed a golden whisk. She filled her lungs with sweet meadow air. Looking at the treats, a tickle of doubt arrived. How to give scores that felt right?

A badger offered a golden apple tart. Crisp crust crackled, sweet apple scent rising like a small kitchen. “Wonderful.” Her pen danced. “The crust, a golden hug. The apples, sweet as a whispered tune.” Were those scores, or poems?

Noor’s carrot cake wore tiny sugared daisies, light as a happy dream. One bite was a soft cloud. “A fluffy cloud, a joyful leap.” Miss Penny’s buns were soft and smelled like warm kitchens. “Each bun, a cozy sigh, a perfect gentle heap.”

Other bakers looked puzzled. “A golden hug? Is that good?” whispered a mole. “A cozy sigh?” A dormouse’s whiskers drooped. Confusion drifted like mist. Etta’s heart sank. The scorecards looked like verses, and verses were not numbers, and numbers were what a bake-off was supposed to understand.

A little field mouse shyly presented a lopsided cake. Not perfect. The icing had slid toward one side as if it had grown tired. One sugared crumb clung to the plate like a small apology. Etta knew the mouse had tried its very best. It tasted of kindness, and of the hour spent stirring when the batter would not agree. Her pen hovered. A pang. The scorebox on the card waited for a number and received, instead, a pause.

Noor hopped closer. “Your poems made me smile. They made me feel happy.” Miss Penny nodded. “Seen — not just for how perfect the bakes were, but for the feeling we put in.”

Etta’s ears perked. Seen. The theme was the heart in each creation: effort, joy, care. Another breath of meadow air, less shaky.

She turned to the bakers, voice clear and kind. “Your apple tart was a warm hug on a chilly day. The sweetness told a happy story.” To the mouse: “Your cake tastes like kindness and happy effort. That is the best flavour there is.”

Numbers were one part. Joy and effort, love stirred into batter, counted too. Noor’s cake a joyful dance. Miss Penny’s buns cozy sighs. The mole stopped whispering. The dormouse’s whiskers lifted.

The fog lifted. Bakers beamed. Effort, creativity, joy — celebrated, understood. The lopsided cake sat in the middle of the table as if it had earned the place, which it had.

Sun dipped, orange and pink. Etta, Noor, and Miss Penny shared the sunny cake, daisies and all. The badger’s tart went round after, still a golden hug. The Bake-Off was not ribbons or perfect scores. It was smiles, silly poetry, the warm sweet feeling of trying your best and being appreciated together. The mole asked, later, whether a hug could be a score, and Etta said yes, if the crust said so first.

She logged golden-hug / lopsided-kindness / poems-as-scores in the judge’s book, left the mouse a daisy from Noor’s cake, and let Miss Penny count blueberries aloud one more time, ten, which was a number and also a kind of poem. That, Etta thought, heart light, was the most beautiful score of all.
